html:
The third emperor of the Mughal Empire, who reigned from 1556 to 1605. He conquered most of north India, built a strong central government, ended the tax on non-Muslims, and welcomed debate between faiths.

He was born in exile in Sindh while his father, Humayun, was on the run from Sher Shah Suri. He came to the throne at thirteen, with the general Bairam Khan as regent. Months later the Mughals defeated the Hindu general Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat, which secured the throne.

His conquests added Malwa, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Bengal, Kashmir and part of the Deccan. Rather than just conquer the Rajput kings, he married into their families and gave them high posts in his army.

How he ruled:

  • He ranked his nobles and officers by the number of horsemen they had to keep, the mansabdari system, and paid many of them with the revenue of assigned lands.
  • His minister Todar Mal measured the land and fixed taxes by its average yield.
  • In 1564 he abolished the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims, and also the tax on Hindu pilgrims.

He built a new capital at Fatehpur Sikri and there, from 1575, held debates among Sunni and Shia scholars, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuit priests from Goa. He promoted "peace with all" and gathered a small circle of followers around his own ideas, later called the Din-i Ilahi. Orthodox clergy hated this.

His court was a centre of painting, music and translation of Sanskrit works into Persian. His friend Abul Fazl wrote the history of his reign, the Akbarnama. His son Jahangir succeeded him.
sum: The third emperor of the Mughal Empire, who reigned from 1556 to 1605. He conquered most of north India, built a strong central government, ended the tax on non-Muslims, and welcomed debate between faiths.
